title: Sony Music moves to add more than 30,000 copyrighted recordings to its lawsuit against Udio

reading.body:
The core failure here is a deployment condition mismatch: Udio built and released a generative music system trained on recordings it did not have rights to use, then made that system publicly available to millions of users before securing any licensing agreements with rights holders. The alleged unauthorized use of copyrighted material happened at the training stage, before any generated output reached a user, meaning the problem was embedded in the system's foundation rather than in a specific output or interaction.

The lawsuits from Universal Music Group, Warner Music Group, Sony Music, and a class of independent artists all center on the same allegation, that copyrighted recordings were copied into training data without permission. Sony's second lawsuit specifically alleges more than 30,000 recordings were used. None of these cases have produced a final verdict, and allegations in a lawsuit are not proven findings of fact.

What it would have taken to catch this at the source is a rights-clearance process applied to training data before model training began, the same kind of licensing negotiation that the post-settlement platform is now being built around. The UMG and WMG settlements, which converted adversarial lawsuits into licensing partnerships, show that a compliant path existed but was not taken at the outset.

summary:
Universal Music Group has settled a lawsuit against AI music startup Udio, reaching licensing agreements to resolve disputes over copyright infringement. UMG had accused Udio of using copyrighted songs to train its artificial intelligence system, including The Temptations' hit "My Girl." Under the settlement, Udio will launch a new platform next year that uses only authorized and licensed music, allowing users to create original compositions from text prompts while artists receive compensation for their work.

The collaboration marks Udio's first licensing deal with a major music label and represents an effort to balance AI innovation with artist protection. UMG's leadership stated the agreements demonstrate commitment to supporting artists while embracing new technologies and business models. Udio declined to disclose financial terms, and specifics about artist compensation remain undisclosed. Founded in 2024 by former Google DeepMind employees, Udio has attracted millions of users and backing from notable investors including musician will.i.am and venture capital firm Andreessen Horowitz.
